prompt: Why are plane waves a natural basis for crystals?

options.text: They repeat with the cell, just like the crystal
options.why: Plane waves compatible with the lattice have the periodicity built in.
Tempting from chemistry, but plane waves fill the whole cell and are not tied to atoms.
Tempting, but there are infinitely many; a cutoff selects a finite set.

hints: Think about what repeats in a crystal.
A wave that fits the cell repeats in every cell.

prompt: In the plane-wave picture, what do the short-wavelength waves describe?

options.text: Fine detail, such as rapid variation near the nuclei
options.why: Short waves change quickly in space, so they capture sharp features.
Tempting, but the broad shape comes from the long waves.
Tempting, but that is fixed by the occupations, not the waves.

hints: Overtones add detail to a sound.
Which waves change fastest in space?

prompt: Why do short plane waves carry more kinetic energy?

options.text: Kinetic energy grows with the square of the wavevector
options.why: Shorter wavelength means larger |k + G| and energy (hbar^2/2m)|k + G|^2.
Tempting, but a basis function has no electrons of its own.

options.text: They do not; all plane waves have the same energy
options.why: Tempting, but the energy depends on the wavevector.

hints: Recall the de Broglie relation from module 2.

prompt: Which statements about a plane-wave basis are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The same basis works for any element
options.why: Plane waves do not depend on which atoms are present.

options.text: Its quality is controlled by one number, the cutoff
options.why: That is a key practical advantage.

options.text: It describes the wiggles near nuclei cheaply
options.why: Tempting, but those need very short waves; pseudopotentials avoid them.

options.text: Forces need no Pulay correction from basis functions moving with atoms
options.why: Plane waves do not move with the atoms, unlike atom-centred bases.

hints: What depends on the atoms, and what does not?
The core region is the expensive part.

prompt: What does ENCUT control?

options.text: The kinetic-energy cutoff that decides which plane waves are kept
options.why: Every wave with energy below ENCUT is kept.
Tempting because both are counts, but electrons come from the POTCAR (NELECT).
Tempting, but that is the KPOINTS file or KSPACING.

hints: It is an energy in eV.

prompt: The largest ENMAX among your POTCARs is 400 eV. What ENCUT does the protocol use?
hints: The protocol multiplies the largest ENMAX by 1.3.

prompt: You raise ENCUT from 400 to 600 eV. Roughly how does the number of plane waves change?

options.text: It grows by about (600/400)^(3/2), close to 1.8 times
options.why: The count grows as ENCUT to the 3/2 power.
Tempting as the ratio of cutoffs, but the waves fill a sphere in 3D.
Tempting because the cell is the same, but the sphere is bigger.

hints: The kept waves fill a sphere.
The radius goes as the square root of ENCUT.

prompt: Why must ENCUT be the same in calculations whose energies you compare?

options.text: Each ENCUT has its own basis-set error, which cancels only if it is the same
options.why: Differences at equal ENCUT converge much faster than absolute energies.
Tempting, but VASP accepts any ENCUT; the danger is silent.

options.text: Because ENCUT changes the number of atoms
options.why: Tempting, but atoms come from the POSCAR.

hints: An energy difference subtracts two errors.

prompt: What is Pulay stress?

options.text: An artificial stress from an incomplete basis when the cell volume changes
options.why: With a fixed set of plane waves, the basis quality depends on the volume.

options.text: The real pressure inside a crystal
options.why: Tempting, but it is an artefact, not physics.

options.text: Stress caused by too many k-points
options.why: Tempting, but it comes from the plane-wave cutoff.

hints: It is named after a basis-set effect.

prompt: In which runs does Pulay stress matter most?

options.text: Relaxations that change the cell shape or volume (ISIF = 3) and elastic runs
options.why: These depend on the stress, which converges slowly with ENCUT.
Tempting, but the stress is not used to change anything there.
Tempting, but the cell is fixed and stress is not used.

hints: The cell must be allowed to change.

prompt: A cell relaxation at a low ENCUT gives a volume that is...

options.why: At fixed plane-wave number the basis worsens as the volume grows, so the cell is pulled smaller.
Tempting, but the artefact favours the smaller cell.
Tempting, but stress converges slowly with ENCUT.

hints: Which volume has the better basis at fixed wave count?
Smaller cell, same waves, finer description.

prompt: Why does the protocol use 1.3 x ENMAX rather than ENMAX?

options.text: The default cutoff often has to be raised by about 30 % to converge the stress
options.why: This is the VASP wiki note the handbook cites.

options.text: ENMAX is a minimum that VASP rejects
options.why: Tempting, but VASP accepts ENMAX; the problem is the stress.
Tempting, but a higher cutoff is slower.

hints: Stress converges more slowly than energy.

prompt: What is the first Brillouin zone?

options.text: The cell of reciprocal space that contains every distinct k label once
options.why: All other k are equivalent to one inside it.
Tempting, but that is a real-space idea.

options.text: The unit cell of the crystal
options.why: Tempting, but it lives in reciprocal space.

hints: k labels repeat in reciprocal space.
It is the set of points closest to Gamma.

prompt: You double the real-space cell length along one direction. What happens to the Brillouin zone along that direction?

options.why: Reciprocal lengths go as one over real-space lengths.
Tempting, but real and reciprocal space are inverse.
Tempting, but the reciprocal lattice depends on the cell.

hints: b = 2 pi / a in one dimension.

prompt: What point is at the centre of every Brillouin zone?

options.why: The zone is built around Gamma.

prompt: What does the label k on an electron state tell you?

options.text: How the phase of the orbital changes from one cell to the next
options.why: Bloch states pick up a phase exp(i k R) between cells.
Tempting, but the energy depends on k and the band index.

options.text: Which atom the electron is on
options.why: Tempting, but Bloch states spread over the crystal.

hints: Each cell looks the same up to a phase.

prompt: Why does VASP use a finite mesh of k-points?

options.text: Averages over the zone are approximated by weighted sums over sample points
options.why: The mesh replaces an integral by a sum.

options.text: Because only those k-points exist in a real crystal
options.why: Tempting, but k is continuous in a large crystal.
Tempting, but that is ENCUT.

prompt: Which materials need the densest k-point meshes?

options.why: Occupations jump across the Fermi surface inside the zone, which converges slowly.
Tempting because gaps are interesting, but their filled bands vary smoothly.
Tempting, but a big box has a tiny zone; Gamma alone often suffices.

prompt: An 8 x 8 x 8 mesh has 512 points but VASP reports far fewer k-points. Why?

options.text: Symmetry: equivalent points are computed once and given larger weights
options.why: Only irreducible points are calculated.

options.text: VASP drops points it cannot converge
options.why: Tempting, but no points are dropped for convergence reasons.

options.text: The mesh was too dense and VASP reduced it
options.why: Tempting, but VASP uses the mesh you gave.

prompt: Your primitive cell converges with a 12 x 12 x 12 mesh. A supercell is 3 times longer along a only. How many points along a keep the same density?
hints: The zone shrinks along a by the same factor.

prompt: What is the difference between a Gamma-centred mesh and a Monkhorst-Pack mesh with an even number of points?

options.text: The even MP mesh is shifted off Gamma; the Gamma-centred mesh contains it
options.why: With VASP's formula, even N does not include k = 0.

options.text: They have different numbers of points
options.why: Tempting, but N x N x N is the same count.

options.text: MP meshes only work for cubic cells
options.why: Tempting, but both work for any cell; symmetry is the issue.

prompt: Which mesh is the safe choice for a hexagonal cell?

options.why: Shifted (even MP) meshes break hexagonal symmetry.

options.text: Monkhorst-Pack with an even number of points
options.why: Tempting as the "standard" mesh, but it breaks the six-fold symmetry.

options.text: Any mesh: symmetry does not matter
options.why: Tempting, but broken symmetry gives more irreducible points and possibly wrong results.

hints: Which mesh keeps the zone centre?

prompt: With VASP's Monkhorst-Pack formula k = (2r - N - 1)/(2N), what is the first coordinate (r = 1) for N = 4?
The author's handbook says "odd MP meshes on hexagonal cells" are a mistake. What does the site's test show?

options.text: It is the even MP meshes that break hexagonal symmetry; odd ones include Gamma
options.why: Recorded as Q-017, an erratum awaiting the author's confirmation.

options.text: Odd MP meshes break the symmetry, as written

Tempting, but even meshes were shown to break it.

prompt: Why do plane-wave codes use pseudopotentials?

options.text: The wiggles of orbitals near the nucleus would need an enormous cutoff
options.why: Replacing the core region by a smooth potential makes the cutoff practical.

options.text: Because core electrons do not exist
options.why: Tempting, but they exist; they are frozen, not removed from physics.

options.text: To make the calculation more accurate than all-electron
options.why: Tempting, but a pseudopotential is an approximation.

prompt: In the PAW lab, what happens when you increase r_c?

options.text: The pseudo function gets smoother, so fewer plane waves are needed, but it is less transferable
options.why: That is the basic trade-off of any pseudopotential.
Tempting, but the all-electron curve is the reference and stays fixed.

options.text: The pseudo function gets more nodes
options.why: Tempting, but the pseudo function is nodeless inside r_c by construction.

hints: Transferability: does it work in other environments?
